seventh_day_adventist.open_canon:
Seventh-day Adventists hold that the biblical canon is closed. The sixty-six books of Scripture are the only rule of faith and practice, the standard by which every teaching and every claimed gift must be tested. We do not add another testament beside the Bible.

What we call the Spirit of Prophecy is the New Testament gift of prophecy at work in the church, most clearly in the ministry of Ellen G. White. Her writings are received as a continuing and authoritative source of counsel, comfort, instruction, and correction for the remnant people. They are not a sixty-seventh book. They point back to Scripture and are themselves judged by it. Members differ in how closely they read her books, but official teaching is that the Bible remains first and last.
seventh_day_adventist.continuing_revelat:
Adventists believe public revelation in the sense of a new biblical canon has ended. The Scriptures are sufficient to make us wise unto salvation. At the same time we believe the Holy Spirit still gives spiritual gifts to the church until the Lord returns, and that one of those gifts is prophecy.

We speak of this as the Spirit of Prophecy. It does not reopen the canon or place a later writer on the same shelf as Isaiah or Paul. It applies the already given Word, warns, and builds up the body. Ellen G. White is received as the Lord's messenger in that sense. Claims of vision or extra-biblical authority that contradict Scripture are rejected. Some Adventists emphasize her writings more than others, but the church's stated position is that the prophetic gift serves the Bible rather than replacing it.
seventh_day_adventist.prophetic_authorit:
Among the gifts of the Spirit listed in Scripture is prophecy. Adventists take this gift to be an identifying mark of the remnant church described in Revelation, and we believe it was manifested in the life and work of Ellen G. White. We call that ministry the Spirit of Prophecy.

Her authority is real for us as guidance to the church, not as a second Bible. She herself directed readers to the Scriptures as the test of all teaching. Official statements describe her writings as a continuing and authoritative source of truth that provide comfort, guidance, instruction, and correction, while insisting that the Bible is the standard. Individual members vary in how they weigh particular passages in her books, yet the church does not treat disagreement with a White paragraph as equivalent to rejecting Scripture.
seventh_day_adventist.sabbath:
The Sabbath is the seventh day of the week, from sunset Friday to sunset Saturday. God blessed and sanctified that day at Creation, before there was a Jewish nation, and the fourth commandment of the unchangeable Decalogue requires its observance as a day of rest, worship, and ministry.

Jesus is Lord of the Sabbath and kept it. Adventists therefore do not treat Sunday as the biblical Sabbath. The day is a memorial of Creation and a sign of the believer's rest in Christ and of sanctification. We gather for worship, cease ordinary work, and seek to make the hours holy. How strictly families apply details such as cooking or travel can vary, but the church's teaching is that the seventh day itself has not been moved and remains binding as a gift rather than a burden.
seventh_day_adventist.soul_sleep:
Adventists describe the state of the dead as an unconscious sleep until the resurrection. A human being is a living soul, not an immortal spirit housed in a body. When a person dies, thoughts perish; the dead know not anything and do not praise God, haunt the living, or go at once to heaven or hell as conscious persons.

Immortality is a gift bestowed at Christ's coming, first to the righteous in the first resurrection. The wicked are raised later and finally destroyed, not kept alive in endless torment. This teaching, often called soul sleep by others, is for us simply the biblical state of the dead. It rules out communication with the departed and explains why we wait for the resurrection rather than speaking of the faithful as already in glory in a disembodied state.
seventh_day_adventist.investigative_judg:
There is a sanctuary in heaven, the true tabernacle the Lord pitched. After His ascension Christ began His high-priestly ministry there, applying the benefits of the one sacrifice offered at the cross. Adventists believe that in 1844, at the close of the 2300 days of Daniel 8, He entered the second and last phase of that ministry: the investigative judgment, prefigured by the Day of Atonement cleansing of the earthly sanctuary.

This work reviews the lives of those who have professed Christ, first the dead and then the living, and shows before the universe who are in Him and therefore worthy of the first resurrection or of translation. It does not add a second atonement to the cross. When it finishes, human probation closes and the Lord comes. The heavenly sanctuary and this pre-Advent judgment are a distinctive Adventist reading of Daniel and Hebrews; members generally receive it as Fundamental Belief, while discussion continues about how to describe its details.
